title: What is the difference between the Repository pattern and the DAO pattern, and how do they help with abstraction, swappable data stores, and testability?
shortTitle: Repository pattern vs DAO — abstraction and testability?

s1_definition.profdef: The DAO (Data Access Object) pattern abstracts and encapsulates access to a specific data source, exposing persistence operations typically mapped to a single table or entity, close to the storage mechanism. The Repository pattern, from Domain-Driven Design, is a higher-level abstraction that mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers, presenting a collection-like interface for aggregate roots and expressing domain intent rather than storage detail. Both decouple business logic from persistence, enabling swappable stores and easier testing via mocking.
s1_definition.analogy: A DAO is like a specialist filing clerk at National Bank of India who knows exactly which cabinet, drawer, and folder format holds account records — very close to the physical storage. A Repository is like a librarian who gives you a clean collection view: "give me the account for Rajesh" or "find all overdrawn accounts," without you ever knowing whether the data lives in a filing cabinet, a database, or a cloud store. The librarian speaks the language of the business; the clerk speaks the language of the storage.
s1_definition.oneliner: DAO abstracts the data source table-by-table; Repository abstracts the domain as a collection of aggregates — both hide persistence so the store is swappable and testable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The DAO (Data Access Object) pattern abstracts and encapsulates access to a specific data source, exposing persistence operations typically mapped to a single table or entity, close to the storage mechanism. The Repository pattern, from Domain-Driven Design, is a higher-level abstraction that mediates between the domain and data-mapping layers, presenting a collection-like interface for aggregate roots and expressing domain intent rather than storage detail. Both decouple business logic from persistence, enabling swappable stores and easier testing via mocking.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A DAO is like a specialist filing clerk at National Bank of India who knows exactly which cabinet, drawer, and folder format holds account records — very close to the physical storage. A Repository is like a librarian who gives you a clean collection view: "give me the account for Rajesh" or "find all overdrawn accounts," without you ever knowing whether the data lives in a filing cabinet, a database, or a cloud store. The librarian speaks the language of the business; the clerk speaks the language of the storage.

**One line to remember:** DAO abstracts the data source table-by-table; Repository abstracts the domain as a collection of aggregates — both hide persistence so the store is swappable and testable.

sections.s2_technical:
A DAO typically mirrors a table. For example, an AccountDao exposes `insert(Account)`, `findById(String)`, `update(Account)`, `delete(String)`. It is storage-oriented and often contains SQL or JPA calls directly. You might have one DAO per table and compose them in the service layer.

A Repository is domain-oriented and treats persistence as an in-memory collection of aggregate roots. For example, an AccountRepository exposes `findById`, `save`, and domain-intent queries like `findOverdrawnAccounts()` or `findByHolderPan(pan)`. In Spring Data, extending JpaRepository gives you a Repository whose implementation is generated at runtime; you never write the boilerplate.

Both patterns deliver three benefits. Abstraction: business code depends on an interface, not on JDBC, JPA, or a specific vendor, so a change in storage technology does not ripple into services. Swappable store: because callers depend on the interface, you can provide a JPA implementation today and a MongoDB or in-memory implementation tomorrow without touching the service. Testability: you can mock the repository interface in unit tests, so the service logic is tested without a database.

The practical difference in modern Spring applications: Spring Data Repository is the default because it eliminates boilerplate and expresses domain intent, while a hand-written DAO is still useful when you need fine-grained control over SQL, stored procedures, or a non-JPA data source. Many systems use repositories for the common case and drop to a custom DAO (or a repository custom-implementation fragment) for complex queries.

Senior nuances: a Repository in strict DDD manages whole aggregates and enforces that you load and save an aggregate root as a unit, which protects invariants. A DAO does not carry that domain contract. Also, hiding the store behind an interface is only truly swappable if you avoid leaking store-specific types (like JPA entities with lazy proxies) across the boundary — returning DTOs or domain objects keeps the abstraction honest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Our services call JPA directly, so when we considered moving some reads to a document store, the change touched dozens of service classes. We need the business code to depend on an abstraction, not on the storage. This is exactly what Repository/DAO abstraction provides.

Problem 2 — We want to unit-test the overdraft-detection logic without a real database. This is exactly testability through a mockable interface.

Problem 3 — We want the option to back the same AccountRepository with JPA in production and an in-memory map in tests or a different store later. This is exactly the swappable-store benefit.

We will define an AccountRepository domain interface, a JPA implementation, and an in-memory implementation, plus a service that depends only on the interface.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run (uses JpaAccountRepository in production)
java -jar target/repository-pattern-service-1.0.0.jar

# List overdrawn accounts
curl http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/overdrawn

# Unit test uses InMemoryAccountRepository — no DB needed
mvn test -Dtest=OverdraftServiceTest
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: find overdrawn accounts; in production CUR3001 has -5,000.

Step 1 — OverdraftService depends only on the AccountRepository interface. Spring injects the JpaAccountRepository in production because it is the @Repository bean.

Step 2 — overdrawnAccounts calls repo.findOverdrawn. The JPA implementation runs a JPQL query over AccountJpaEntity, maps each result to a pure domain Account via toDomain, and returns a list. No JPA entity leaks out of the repository, so the service works only with domain objects.

Step 3 — The service sees CUR3001 as overdrawn (balance -5,000) because the domain Account's isOverdrawn returns true. It logs a warning and returns the list.

Step 4 — In a unit test, we inject InMemoryAccountRepository instead, seed it with a couple of Account objects, and call overdrawnAccounts. The exact same service code runs with zero database involvement, proving testability and a swappable store.

```
Hibernate: select a.* from accounts a where a.balance < 0
WARNING  Found 1 overdrawn accounts
# In test:
WARNING  Found 1 overdrawn accounts   (InMemory, no DB)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Both the DAO and Repository patterns exist to decouple business logic from persistence, but they sit at different levels. A DAO abstracts a specific data source and is usually organized table by table, exposing storage-oriented operations like insert, update, and delete, and it tends to live close to the SQL or JPA calls. A Repository, which comes from Domain-Driven Design, is a higher-level abstraction that presents a collection-like view of aggregate roots and speaks the language of the domain, so instead of raw CRUD it exposes intent such as find-overdrawn-accounts or find-by-holder-pan. In Spring Data, extending JpaRepository gives me a Repository whose implementation is generated at runtime, which removes the boilerplate a hand-written DAO would carry.

The three benefits both patterns deliver are abstraction, a swappable store, and testability. Abstraction means my services depend on an interface rather than on JDBC, JPA, or a vendor, so changing storage technology does not ripple through the business code. A swappable store follows directly: because callers depend on the interface, I can back it with JPA in production and an in-memory map in tests, or a document store later, without touching the service. Testability means I can mock or substitute the repository in unit tests and exercise the business logic with no database at all.

In our National Bank of India system I define an AccountRepository domain interface with intent-revealing methods, provide a JPA-backed implementation that maps between the JPA entity and a pure domain object, and provide an in-memory implementation for tests. The overdraft-detection service depends only on the interface, so the exact same service code runs against PostgreSQL in production and against a HashMap in a unit test, which makes the overdraft logic fast and trivial to verify.

The senior nuance I stress is that the abstraction is only genuinely swappable if I do not leak store-specific types across the boundary, so my repository returns domain objects or DTOs rather than JPA entities with lazy proxies. In strict DDD the Repository also manages whole aggregates, loading and saving an aggregate root as a unit to protect its invariants, which is a contract a plain DAO does not carry. In practice I use Spring Data repositories for the common case and drop to a custom implementation fragment or a hand-written DAO only when I need fine control over complex SQL, stored procedures, or a non-JPA source.

---

keyPoints: Repository: interface-based, Spring generates implementation at runtime
DAO: class-based, you write the implementation manually
Repository: easier to test — mock the interface
Both achieve: swappable storage, testable service layer
